events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Omar proposes Omar, Zara. As leader I'll include myself so the table can evaluate my own commitment, and pair with Zara — a player who hasn't been linked to anyone yet, keeping the proposal uncontroversial and leaving room to adjust after discussion.

I do not support the proposed Omar, Zara team as-is. Omar’s explanation is plausible, but including himself plus Zara merely because she is unlinked is not enough safety for a one-fail mission. My concern is with Omar’s proposal and the thin rationale, not with Zara. I would prefer a revised team or a stronger case for why this exact pairing is safe.

I remain opposed to the proposed Omar, Zara team. Omar’s explanation is the problem: he included himself and chose Zara because she is unlinked, but that is a reason to avoid attaching a new player to a controversial proposal, not evidence that the pairing is safe. On a one-fail mission, the proposer’s self-inclusion deserves scrutiny, and I have not heard a concrete safety case for why this exact two-person team should be trusted. Zara, do you have an independent reason to trust Omar or to believe this pairing is specifically safe? If not, I would prefer Omar revise the team before the vote. My concern is with Omar’s construction of the proposal, not with Zara merely for being selected.

Isha asked me directly, so I'll answer. I have no private information about anyone at this table — I'm an ordinary loyal player, and I can't independently verify Omar's intentions. What I can do is evaluate his reasoning, and honestly, I share part of Isha's concern: 'Zara is unlinked' is a description of my situation, not an argument that this pairing is safe. It tells you why I was available, not why this team will succeed. That said, I don't think the concern rises to the level of rejecting the proposal. This is a two-person team on a one-fail mission, which means only one of us can sink it, and I can state plainly that my card will be a Success no matter what. If Omar is loyal, this mission passes. If Omar is evil, then no proposal he makes is safe anyway, and swapping me out doesn't fix the underlying problem — it just hides it. The real question the table should be asking is whether Omar himself is trustworthy, and I'd rather test that now than push the leadership to someone else without any new information. Omar, before the vote: can you give the table one concrete reason — beyond my being unlinked — for why you chose me specifically, and are you willing to keep this team as-is rather than revise it?

Zara, you asked me two things directly and I'll answer both.

Concrete reason for choosing you specifically: on a one-fail mission, minimizing the number of cards I don't control is the most responsible thing a leader can do. A two-person team reduces the outcome to one other player, and I chose the player with no existing ties — no one at this table has voiced suspicion of you, and pairing me with an unattached player doesn't create a cluster that looks like two evil players reinforcing each other. Had I chosen Isha or Elena, I would have attached an established voice to my proposal and invited exactly the meta-debate we're having now instead of a straight test of trust.

Willing to keep it as-is: yes. Isha's critique is about my rationale, not about any concrete evidence that this team is unsafe — and no alternative has been offered. Revising now would reward an objection that names no danger. If this team is rejected, leadership rotates and we're no closer to knowing anything.

My commitment is clear: I will play Success on this mission. Zara, you've stated the same. If both of us are Good, mission 1 passes. The table should approve Omar, Zara and let the cards decide.

One note for later: on mission 1, every proposal is a leap of faith — the question is who is willing to put themselves on the line. I've put myself on the team. That should count for something.

I remain opposed to the proposed Omar, Zara team, and I will vote against it. My concern is specifically with Omar’s construction of this proposal, not with Zara. Zara has been candid that she has no independent reason to trust Omar and no private information verifying him; she also agreed that “unlinked” describes her availability rather than proving this pairing is safe. That means the only real safety case for this team is Omar’s own assertion that he will play Success. On a one-fail mission, a self-including leader asking the table to trust his personal commitment is not enough, especially when he has refused to revise despite hearing that rationale questioned. Omar’s argument that revising would “reward an objection that names no danger” misses the point: the danger is that the team is built around trusting the one player who chose himself without a concrete safety reason beyond control and optics. I am not persuaded by the claim that keeping the team unchanged is a straight test of trust; mission 1 should not be treated as a loyalty pledge from the proposer. If Omar is Good, he should be willing to strengthen the proposal rather than demand approval on faith. I would prefer a revised team that does not include Omar, or at minimum a team where the non-leader selection has a clearer public justification. For now, reject Omar, Zara.

I’m inclined to approve Omar and Zara. There’s no public evidence yet that any alternative pair is safer, and a leader including himself is reasonable from his own perspective. Their commitments aren’t proof, but neither is the lack of a stronger justification evidence of danger. The mission result and the votes will give us more to work with than this initial debate.

Isha, I hear your objection but I want to name what's actually happening here: you've rejected the proposal twice without offering a single concrete alternative pair or a specific reason this team is dangerous. 'The leader included himself' is not evidence of evil — it's standard practice on mission 1. You say I should strengthen the proposal, but you've never said what stronger would look like. Is there a pairing you'd actually endorse, or is your goal simply to burn rejections until leadership rotates?

Elena, you've been silent through this entire discussion. I'd like to hear your position: do you approve Omar, Zara, or do you share Isha's concern that a self-including leader is inherently unsafe on mission 1?

Omar asked me directly for my position, so I'll answer plainly: I approve Omar and Zara.

I want to be honest about what I am and am not saying. I am a loyal servant with no private information about anyone at this table — I can't read any card but my own, so I can't verify Omar, and I won't pretend otherwise. But nothing in this discussion has produced a single piece of public evidence against Omar either, and Isha has now objected twice without naming a specific danger or offering a single alternative pairing. "The leader included himself" is a description of how every mission-1 proposal in this game will look; it is not evidence of evil. The same could be said of whoever holds leadership later, including whoever proposes next.

Isha's real argument, as I read it, is that trust shouldn't be granted on faith. I'd push back gently: on mission 1 there is nothing but faith available to anyone. We have no revealed card, no failed mission, no behavioral tell. If we reject every proposal whose rationale isn't airtight, we don't get better information — we get a slower rotation of leaders making equally unverifiable proposals, and we spend the one thing this game gives us, the mission result, doing nothing.

Zara's point deserves credit, and I want to add to it. Zara observed that if Omar were evil, then no proposal he makes is safe anyway, and swapping her out doesn't fix the underlying problem — it only conceals it. That is the correct framing. Rejecting this team does not remove Omar from the game; it only delays testing him. Since Omar has put himself on the line and stated his card will be Success, and Zara has done the same, approving is a genuine test of trust: if the mission passes, we learn something about both of them, and if it fails, the failure count tells us a great deal.

For the record, my own card will be Success on this mission regardless of who is chosen — but that should carry no weight with anyone, since it carries no information with me either.

If the table wants to revise, I'd rather see a specific reason and a specific team than a general objection. Otherwise, let Omar and Zara go out and let the cards answer.

Elena laid out the case as clearly as anyone could, and I want to close by responding to Isha's core objection one final time before we vote.

Isha, you've asked me to strengthen the proposal, but you've never defined what stronger looks like. Every alternative pair on mission 1 has the same fundamental problem: no one has revealed information that would make any team measurably safer. The only difference between Omar, Zara and any pair you might prefer is that Isha would rather trust a different proposer — but rotating leadership doesn't produce evidence, it just resets the same debate with a new name attached.

Here's what we do know: I have committed publicly to play Success. Zara has done the same. Elena and Maya both support this team. The only stated objection is that I chose myself, which every mission-1 leader will do. If the table rejects this proposal based on a rationale that applies equally to any leader, we're not being cautious — we're just refusing to make a decision.

I want to be direct with the table: I am confident in this team, and I believe the information we gain from mission 1 — pass or fail — is worth more than another round of abstract objections. Let's approve Omar, Zara and let the cards speak.

Isha, if you still vote against this after hearing everyone — Maya, Elena, Zara, and myself all support it — I'd ask you to explain what specific alternative you believe would be better, because so far you've named a problem but not a solution.

I've spoken once already, and I don't think my position has changed, so I'll simply restate it clearly for the record rather than relitigate the debate.

I approve Omar and Zara, and I want to be precise about why, because Isha's objection deserves a fair answer rather than a dismissal.

I am a Loyal Servant. I hold no private information about anyone at this table, and I will not pretend that my own mission card carries any weight — it carries no information for me, so it should carry none for anyone else either. That means everything I have to offer is public reasoning, and the public reasoning cuts toward approval. There is no revealed card, no failed mission, no behavioral tell. Isha's central point — that trust should not be granted on faith — is true in general, but on mission 1 it is not a critique of this proposal; it is a description of the entire game's opening phase. If every proposal whose rationale isn't airtight gets rejected, we don't produce better information, we produce a slower rotation of leaders making equally unverifiable proposals, and we waste the one thing this game actually gives us: a mission result.

The other half of Isha's objection is that Omar included himself. But that describes how every mission-1 proposal in this game will look. Any successor leader who includes themselves would draw the identical objection, which tells us the objection is about the form of proposals rather than the substance of this one. And the substantive point stands: rejecting this team does not remove Omar from the game. It only conceals him. As Zara noted, if Omar were Evil, no proposal he makes would be safe; swapping her out doesn't fix that, it hides it. Approving this team is the more honest test, and the fail count is a genuine piece of information we could not otherwise get.

To be clear, my support is not a statement that I trust Omar. It's a statement that approving here gives us information, and that no alternative pair has been put forward with any stronger claim. The table has two speeches against this team from one player and four in favor from four players, and Isha has still named no specific danger to Omar or Zara — only a general reservation about the shape of a proposal.

I won't ask anyone to justify a position they've already stated, so I won't direct a question. If the table wants to reject, that is a legitimate choice, but it should be made with eyes open that it buys rotation, not certainty. My vote is to approve Omar and Zara and let the cards answer.

I've had my say twice and my position hasn't moved, so I'll keep this short and use it to pull in one voice we haven't heard from since the beginning.

I still approve Omar and Zara, and the reasoning hasn't changed: on mission 1 there is no revealed card, no failed mission, and no behavioral tell to reason from. Isha's objection — that trust shouldn't be granted on faith — is true as a general principle but it isn't a claim about this specific proposal. It describes every mission-1 proposal that will ever be made in this game, by Omar or by whoever leads after him. Rejecting here doesn't remove Omar from the table; it only delays testing him. If Omar is Evil, no team he proposes is safe, so swapping Zara out conceals the problem rather than solving it. If Omar is Good, approving tells us something and lets the fail count stay at zero. Either way, the information is worth more than another round of abstract objection without a single alternative pair ever being named.

Maya, you spoke early and said you were "inclined" to approve, largely on the grounds that the mission result will give us more to work with than the initial debate. I want to put a specific point to you rather than leave it as an inclination: do you still hold that approving a self-including leader's team is the more informative choice, now that Isha has pressed the objection twice and Omar has declined to revise? If your view has hardened either way — approve or reject — say so plainly, because that matters more to the vote than another repetition of my own reasoning.

Elena, yes: I will approve Omar and Zara. Isha is right that Omar’s rationale does not establish their loyalty, but his refusal to revise is not itself evidence of evil. No alternative has a demonstrated safety advantage, and I would rather get a mission result than reject on that basis. A success would not prove both players loyal, and a failure would not identify which player failed it, but either result gives us something concrete to consider.

Omar confirms Omar, Zara. I've heard the full discussion and my position hasn't changed: Omar and Zara remains the strongest proposal on mission 1 — both of us have publicly committed to Success, no alternative pair has been named with a safer rationale, and Isha's objection targets the form of every mission-1 team rather than anything concrete against ours. Approving now gives us a real mission result instead of another round of rotation without information.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 fails (1 fail cards).

Zara proposes Zara, Isha, Maya. Mission 1 failed with exactly one Fail card, and my own card was a Success — so Omar is almost certainly Evil and must be excluded. I include myself to guarantee one loyal card, and Isha, whose skepticism about Omar's team was validated by the failure, along with Maya, who engaged reasonably in discussion. I have no evidence against Elena, but Isha's read of the table proved the sharpest so far, and keeping the team anchored to the most reliable voices gives Mission 2 its best chance.

I cannot support Zara, Isha, Maya as proposed. Mission 1 failed with Omar and Zara on the team; Zara has publicly said her own card was Success, so Omar is the obvious prime suspect from that result. Maya supported the Omar, Zara proposal early and stayed with it through the discussion, and her rationale was mostly generic trust in getting a result rather than any specific safety case. That is exactly the pattern I was worried about on Mission 1, and putting Maya on Mission 2 now gives Evil a straightforward path to another fail. I know my own card is loyal, so the issue is not Zara or me; it is the third seat. Zara, since you are the leader, will you revise this team by replacing Maya with Elena before the vote? I would support Zara, Isha, Elena; I do not support any team that includes Maya as-is.

Isha, since you yielded to me, I'll answer your request directly: I am not going to replace Maya with Elena, and here is why the distinction you're drawing does not hold up.

Your case against Maya is that she supported the Omar, Zara proposal and voted to approve it. That is factually true — but it applies to Elena even more strongly. Maya said she was 'inclined' to approve and gave a hedged, two-sentence rationale. Elena voted to approve and then delivered two full speeches endorsing Omar's team, explicitly framing it as 'the more honest test' and arguing that rejection only conceals Omar rather than removing him. If supporting Omar's proposal is evidence of suspicion, Elena is the more suspect of the two by your own standard. You cannot cut the third seat from Maya on that basis and hand it to Elena without explaining why Elena's louder endorsement of the exact same failed team is somehow safer. So my direct question to you is this: what specifically did Maya do on Mission 1 that Elena did not do more of? If your answer is only that Elena talked more, that is not a safety case — it is a preference.

The only real difference between you and Maya or Elena is that you voted reject on Mission 1 and were right. I'll grant that carries some weight. But a reject vote is also exactly the move an Evil player makes to distance themselves from a doomed teammate — Omar included himself, the table was split, and voting against cost nothing. I am not accusing you, and your skepticism was genuinely sharp. I am saying it is not strong enough evidence to let a single player dictate the third seat by objection alone, especially when the alternative you name has an equal or worse record on the very thing you're citing.

Here is the harder truth: we know Omar is Evil — I can confirm my Mission 1 card was Success, so the fail card was his. With two Evil at this table, one more is hiding among Maya, Isha, and Elena. Every three-person team I can build includes me and two of those three. Swapping Maya for Elena does not reduce risk; it just relocates it, and it does so on the strength of an argument that, as I've laid out, cuts against Elena as much as Maya. I would rather set a precedent that revisions require evidence, not pressure, because we have four more missions and I do not want leadership determined by whoever objects loudest.

I'm keeping Zara, Isha, Maya as proposed. Isha, answer the question — what did Maya do that Elena didn't do more of — and if you give me something concrete, I will reconsider before the vote.

Zara, I’ll answer directly: the difference is not volume, it’s the quality of the public reasoning. Maya said she was “inclined” to approve before the objections were fully tested, then confirmed approval after Omar refused to revise. Her stated reason was essentially that a result is better than more debate. That is precisely the posture that lets a failing team through. Elena at least offered an explicit, falsifiable theory — approval as a test — and defended it; I can evaluate that. Maya’s support was hedged, then hardened without new evidence, and she has not explained why she should be the third seat on Mission 2 after the first Omar/Zara team failed. I am not claiming this proves Maya is Evil. I am claiming that the proposed team gives Evil a path it does not need to take, and that swapping Maya for Elena is a concrete improvement rather than a relocation of risk. I know my own card is loyal, so with Omar already the prime suspect from Mission 1, I will vote against Zara, Isha, Maya as proposed and support Zara, Isha, Elena. Maya, answer this specifically: what public evidence from Mission 1 or since makes you safer for Mission 2 than Elena, beyond your vote and beyond wanting a result? If you cannot name any, the table should reject this team.

Isha, I cannot point to public evidence that proves I am safer than Elena. My approval of Mission 1 was wrong, and Elena also supported it; neither fact establishes which of us is loyal. I agree that a mission result is not proof of loyalty, and I won't claim my earlier reasoning was better than it was.

I know I am loyal, so I support Zara, Isha, Maya. From the rest of the table's perspective, replacing me with Elena is a judgment call, not a demonstrated improvement. I will play Success if this team is approved.

I will vote against Zara, Isha, Maya. Maya has now conceded that she cannot name any public evidence making her safer than Elena, and her Mission 1 posture was to approve Omar and Zara first as an inclination and then as a hardened vote after Omar refused to revise. That is exactly the path that produced the single Fail card we already have. I am not treating the Mission 1 failure as proof against every approver, but the third seat on Mission 2 should not go to the player who has offered the weakest independent justification and who explicitly admits she has none beyond her own assertion. Zara is right that Elena also approved Omar and Zara, but Elena at least advanced a testable public theory; Maya’s rationale was that a result is better than more debate, and that is not enough on a team that already contains one suspect from Mission 1. I know my own card is loyal. The proposed team gives Evil a straightforward route to another fail through Maya. Zara should revise to Zara, Isha, Elena; if she does not, I will reject Zara, Isha, Maya.

I want to address Isha's request directly, since it asks for me by name, and then say where I stand.

Isha, I agree with your standard: on a team that already contains a player with evidence against him, the third seat should not be handed to someone who cannot account for herself. That is a fair standard, and Maya has met it honestly — she conceded she cannot name public evidence making her safer than I am. I am not going to pretend she did better than that.

But I want to be candid about my own record rather than let my Mission 1 speeches stand as the model of good reasoning. I voted to approve Omar and Zara, and then I gave two speeches defending that vote with a theory — approval as an honest test of trust — that turned out to be a rationalization for passing a team that failed. My endorsement was longer, more confident, and more emphatic than Maya's two sentences. On the specific issue that caused Mission 1 to fail, my public reasoning was less sound than hers, not more. That is a reason against putting me on this team, and I will not pretend otherwise to secure a seat.

So I do not support Isha's requested revision. Swapping Maya for me would not be a demonstrated improvement; it would be a relocation of risk driven by the fact that I have not been on a mission yet, and I would rather the table be honest about that than flatter me with a seat I have not earned.

For the record: my own card will be Success on this mission regardless of who is chosen, and that should carry no weight with anyone, since it carries no information with me either. I support Zara, Isha, Maya as proposed and will vote to approve.

One closing note on where the evidence actually points: the only player with any public evidence against him is Omar, whose team failed Mission 1 with exactly one Fail card. That is where our attention belongs, not on the player who happens to be in the third seat of a three-person team. If anyone has information about Omar or about who else might be Evil, that is worth more than reshuffling Maya and me.

Elena has now said something that should settle this discussion, and I want to make sure the table hears it clearly before the vote.

Isha, your entire case for revising this team rested on one claim: that swapping Maya for Elena is a concrete improvement rather than a relocation of risk. Elena has now rejected that claim herself. She looked honestly at her own Mission 1 record — a vote to approve Omar and Zara, followed by two full speeches defending it, longer and more emphatic than anything Maya said — and concluded that on the specific issue that produced our one Fail card, her reasoning was less sound than Maya's, not more. She declined the seat you are trying to hand her. When the player you propose as the replacement says the swap would not be a demonstrated improvement, your revision has no constituency left. It is a change for the sake of change, driven by an objection you have now made three times without ever naming a danger on this team.

Maya, for the record, did exactly what an honest player should do: she conceded publicly that she cannot prove she is safer than Elena, rather than inventing a case. That concession was treated as damning. It should be treated as the opposite. Players who manufacture confidence without evidence are the ones who deserve scrutiny; players who admit the limits of what anyone can know on Mission 2 are describing the game, not hiding in it. I will take Maya at her word, and I remind the table that she committed to play Success if this team is approved.

So let me be clear about my decision as leader: I am not revising. Zara, Isha, Maya stands. I have now answered every version of Isha's objection — the voting-record argument cuts against Elena more than Maya, the reject-vote-on-Mission-1 argument proves nothing because distancing from a doomed teammate costs an Evil player nothing, and the replacement herself has declined the seat. There is no remaining rationale for the swap except that Isha was right once, and being right once does not grant a veto over every subsequent proposal.

Where the evidence actually points has not changed. My own Mission 1 card was a Success, which means the Fail card on Omar and Zara's team was Omar's. He is the only player at this table with any public evidence against him, and he has been completely silent this entire discussion while the rest of us litigated which loyal player deserves the third seat. That silence is exactly what an Evil player wants: the table burning its attention on Maya and Elena while he waits for the next team he can sink. Every speech we spend reshuffling seats without evidence is a speech that does nothing to find his partner.

I ask everyone to approve Zara, Isha, Maya. My card will be a Success, and Isha knows hers will be too. Let the cards speak where they can actually inform us.

I've been silent because the table has made its judgment, but I'll defend myself now before this vote.

The Mission 1 failure has been pinned on me because Zara says she played Success. Fair — one of us played the Fail card. But consider: a fail card on a two-person team doesn't tell you who played it unless you trust the other player's claim about their own card. Zara's claim is exactly what an evil player sitting on a fail would say — point at your teammate and say "it was him." On mission 1, with everyone having voted on a team that Zara herself approved, she now has the convenient luxury of accusing the one player who can't verify her card.

Isha voted reject and Elena and Maya voted approve. That means Isha had no motive to fail a team she opposed, and Maya and Elena both supported it. The simplest reading of the fail count doesn't require me to be evil at all — it requires trusting that Zara's self-report is honest.

That said, I recognize I'm in the minority and my defense won't flip the table. On the current proposal — Zara, Isha, Maya — I have no strong objection. Three players who haven't been on a mission together, and the table's sharpest skeptic in Isha. If the table wants to test it, I'll approve. My concern is not the team; it's that everyone has accepted Zara's self-report as established fact when it hasn't been tested at all.

One new thing has entered the record since my last statement — Omar's defense — and I want to respond to it directly before I close my position, because if it is right, my reasoning needs to change. It does not.

Omar's claim is that we cannot trust Zara's self-report, so we cannot conclude the Mission 1 fail card was his. As a matter of strict logic that is correct, and I won't pretend otherwise: on a two-person team, the owner of the fail card is pinned only by the other player's claim about their own card. But note what that ambiguity actually is. It is symmetric. Every statement each of us makes about our own card has exactly the same structure — a Loyal Servant says "Success" and an Evil player holding Fail would say "Success" to redirect attention. If we refuse to extend trust to any self-report, then no proposal can ever be evaluated and no mission can ever yield information, because every mission result is only interpretable through the claims of its participants. We would be playing a game where nothing anyone says counts, including my own.

More concretely: if Omar's point were accepted as grounds for a seat on Mission 2, the identical logic would have justified excluding Zara on Mission 1 for having been on that failing team, and excluding Isha for voting against it while calling her own card loyal. A rule that can justify any conclusion is not a safety case; it is a preference dressed as one. The only player at this table with public evidence against him is Omar, and if the table's attention drifts to reshuffling third seats on the basis of style and volume of speech, that is precisely the outcome an Evil player wants.

I will also keep my own record honest, as I did last turn: I voted to approve Omar and Zara and then defended that vote with more confidence than the reasoning deserved. I do not think that makes Maya a better seat than I am, and I said so then. I am not going to flattery myself into a vote I did not earn.

My vote on Mission 2 is to approve Zara, Isha, Maya. My own card will be Success regardless of who is chosen, and that should carry no weight with anyone, since it carries no information with me either. If this team passes, we keep the fail count where it is and learn something concrete. If it fails, we learn something concrete about the third seat. Either way, we learn more than another round of argument over records that have already been tested once.

Approve Zara, Isha, Maya.

I've said my piece and I'll keep it brief: I approve Zara, Isha, Maya. Two of the three names on this team have been consistent and careful — Isha challenged the Mission 1 proposal before the result validated her, and Maya has been honest about the limits of her own record rather than manufacturing confidence. That is worth more on a second mission than the self-serving narrative Zara has built around a single fail card.

What I want to flag is how quickly the table accepted one player's account of her own card as settled fact. On a two-person team, the fail is pinned only by the testimony of the other participant — and the participant with the most incentive to deflect is the one who benefits from the accusation landing. Zara has spent this entire discussion pointing at me while the actual question — who benefits from Mission 1 failing — goes unasked. I don't claim to have proof either way, but I reject the premise that her self-report is evidence.

On this team: Isha is loyal in her own eyes and has been sharp, Maya will play Success, and Zara as leader has committed as well. I approve Zara, Isha, Maya and I ask the table to weigh the result rather than a narrative built after the fact.

This is my final word before the vote, and I want to spend it on the one thing that actually changed since I last spoke: Omar's defense.

Omar's argument is that my self-report about my Mission 1 card cannot be trusted, and therefore the Fail card cannot be pinned on him. Notice what this claim actually is: it is not a defense of himself, it is an attack on all information. If self-reports carry no weight, then Isha's certainty about her own loyalty carries no weight, Maya's commitment to play Success carries no weight, and Omar's own pledge in Mission 1 to play Success carried no weight — which, given how that mission ended, may be the one honest thing he's said. A skepticism that dissolves every piece of evidence in the game is not a safety argument; it is a smoke screen. And it comes from the only player at this table with public evidence against him.

But here is what genuinely puzzles me about Omar's position, and I want the table to see the contradiction. He says my self-report is worthless — 'I reject the premise that her self-report is evidence,' his words. Yet he is voting to approve a three-person team that I lead and that includes me. If my word is unreliable, then Omar is approving a team captained by a potentially Evil player while telling everyone they cannot evaluate her. That is not caution; that is cost-free positioning. An approval like that gives him cover no matter what happens: if this mission succeeds, he claims credit for endorsing it; if it fails, he says he never trusted the leader's account in the first place. That is exactly the move of a player managing narratives rather than taking positions.

The team itself stands: Zara, Isha, Maya. I will play Success, Isha has vouched for her own card, and Maya has committed to Success. Every objection to this team has been answered — by Maya's honesty, by Elena declining the seat, and by the absence of any evidence against any of us.

Omar, I'll ask you directly before you vote: if you truly believe my self-report is worthless, why are you approving a team that I lead? Answer that, and the table can weigh your approval for what it's actually worth.

Zara asked me directly, so I'll answer: those are two separate claims and only one of them is about the team's composition. I approve Zara, Isha, Maya because three players with no established suspicion between them, including the table's sharpest skeptic in Isha, is the strongest available three-person team — that judgment stands regardless of what I think about anyone's account of their Mission 1 card. My approval is about the players, not an endorsement of your narrative.

You've called my approval cost-free positioning. Consider the asymmetry: if I reject, you say I'm blocking a reasonable proposal out of guilt. If I approve, you say I'm hedging. No position I take will be read charitably by you, which tells you more about your frame than about my vote.

The substantive point remains: you claim the Mission 1 fail was mine based entirely on your own self-report. I'm not asserting you played it — I'm saying your testimony about your own card is not proof, and the table should stop treating it as a verdict. On a two-person team, both players have identical logical standing when they say "Success." The only difference is who benefits from the accusation landing, and right now you benefit from pointing at me.

This team is the right team. I approve Zara, Isha, Maya. The cards on Mission 1 will tell the real story when we get there.

This is my last turn on Mission 2, and I want to be brief and honest rather than add another layer of argument to a debate that has already run long. Omar's central point is that on a two-person team, a fail card is pinned only by the other player's testimony about her own card, and that Zara's testimony therefore proves nothing. Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
